newsitem.title: USA: Report ruled inadmissible in Reynolds trial.
newsitem.headline: Report ruled inadmissible in Reynolds trial.

text.p: A Florida judge on Monday ruled a 1988 U.S. Surgeon-General's report on the health effects of smoking inadmissible in a wrongful death lawsuit against RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp's R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co.

Reynolds' attorney had Paul Crist objected to the admission of the Surgeon-General's report, arguing that it was hearsay because it was compiled from research and reports done by a wide range of researchers and not written solely by a government employee.
"These are classic hearsay and double hearsay," he said.

Lawyers for plaintiff Dana Raulerson had wanted to enter the report as evidence during their examination of expert witness Dr. Allan Feingold, a Miami physician who testifed that late smoker Jean Connor was addicted to cigarettes.
Raulerson had filed the lawsuit on behalf of the estate of her sister, Connor, who died of lung cancer in 1995 at age 49.
The six-member jury hearing the case lost a juror and gained another Monday.

A male juror whose kidney stone ailment forced an early end to testimony on Friday was dismissed and replaced with a female alternate. The panel now is made up of five women and one man, leaving a lone female alternate.

Raulerson's attorney, Norwood "Woody" Wilner, succeeded in having the report admitted in a trial last year when he won a $750,000 judgment in a product liability case filed by smoker Grady Carter against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc.
Wilner said the Surgeon General's reports were "classic and precise examples" of government reports.
But Judge Bernard Nachman ruled that the report did not meet the legal standard for admissibility.

Later, Raulerson's legal team downplayed the ruling, saying expert witnesses would still be able to cite from the report and use it to form conclusions about the addictive nature of nicotine. "All it means is that the jury won't get physical possession of it," Wilner co-counsel Greg Maxwell said. "It's not a major setback."
The plaintiff's first and only medical expert witness, Feingold, took the stand for his third day of testimony, telling jurors that Jean Connor was addicted to cigarettes.
She was smoking a pack a day by the time she was 18 and three packs a day when she was 30, he said.

Feingold, who was not involved in treating Connor and draws his conclusions about her condition from examining her medical history, testified that nicotine has a direct effect on the brain and said people use cigarettes as their source of "nicotine hits."
He conceded that not all smokers are addicted and that it was possible to quit smoking, but said even 30 percent of heroin users were able to stop without help.

He said smokers had a tendency to relapse, citing statistics that showed 80 percent of smokers want to stop in any given year and 35 percent try to quit on their own, but at the end of the year only five percent have been able to stay off cigarettes.

Jean Connor's behavior was "that of an addictive person," he said, adding that she smoked despite knowing about the possible health effects and even when she was not feeling well. "She had an addictive pattern of behavior."
